rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation. This should show whether any compounds are unretained early or still only elute during the high-organic hold, guiding the next narrowing or steepening step.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so now optimize time by trimming the gradient window to the observed elution window and making it steeper while raising temperature. This should pull the late peak earlier while likely keeping the current worst pair above 1.5.

The steep 10 min gradient over-compressed the critical 6/7 pair, so keep the successful window and temperature but lengthen tG to recover resolution while staying near the 10 min last-peak target. This directly tests how strongly that pair responds to slope.

The critical pair does not improve with a shallower slope, so it is likely a selectivity problem rather than a slope problem; change temperature instead. Dropping from 50 to 40 C keeps the fast, well-targeted window while testing whether the 6/7 pair reorders or separates better at lower temperature.

You have a perfect score, so now try to shorten the method while watching the critical 6/7 pair that is just above the 1.5 threshold. Keeping the same window and temperature but reducing tG by one step is the most direct way to see if full resolution can be maintained with a faster run.

Since shortening tG hurt the critical pair, return to the resolved 10 min slope and instead try a slightly narrower, lower high-organic endpoint to improve selectivity around the mid-eluting cluster while still keeping the last peak inside 10 min. This tests whether the 6/7 pair benefits from a shifted phi window without sacrificing the perfect score.

The perfect method at 40 C has only a small margin on the critical 6/7 pair, and lowering temperature previously improved selectivity versus 50 C. Test 35 C with the proven 10 min, 0.10–0.65 window to see whether that pair gains extra resolution while the last peak stays under 10 min.

The 40 C, 10 min method is already optimal in score, so probe nearby conditions that might preserve full resolution while adding a little retention margin to the last peak region. Raising phi1 one step tests whether a slightly wider window changes selectivity in the crowded middle enough to improve robustness without pushing any peak past 10 min.

The first peak is still fairly early, so raise phi0 one step while keeping the proven window width, slope, and temperature to see whether shifting the whole gradient later can preserve full resolution and keep the last peak under 10 min. This is a targeted robustness test around the current optimum without repeating prior conditions.

This new 0.15–0.65 window gives a slightly better margin on the critical pair than the original perfect method, so now test whether it can support a shorter gradient. Reducing tG to 8 min is the next logical speed optimization while keeping the improved selectivity window and temperature.

The 0.15–0.65 window is perfect and has slightly better critical-pair margin than 0.10–0.65, so now test a slightly narrower high-end to see if selectivity can be maintained or improved while still keeping the last peak under 10 min. This is a local refinement around the best-performing region without changing the proven 10 min slope or temperature.

The 0.15–0.65 method is perfect with slightly improved critical-pair margin, and the first peak is now very close to unretained, so raise phi0 one more step while keeping the rest fixed. This tests whether the window can be shifted upward for a faster, still fully resolved method without losing the 6/7 separation.

The 0.15–0.65 window is perfect, while pushing phi0 to 0.20 made the critical pair fall below 1.5; now test a slightly wider high end from the better 0.15 start. This checks whether added late-gradient range can preserve or improve the 6/7 margin while keeping the last peak comfortably under 10 min.

The best current condition is 0.15–0.65 at 10 min, and its critical pair has only modest margin above 1.5. A slight increase in tG will show whether that pair gains useful robustness at 40 C, helping define the local tradeoff around the optimum even if it slightly sacrifices speed.

The data suggest the optimum lies near higher phi0 and lower phi1, but 0.20–0.65 slightly under-resolved the critical pair while 0.15–0.60 was fully resolved but too slow. Testing 0.20–0.60 at the same 10 min and 40 C probes whether narrowing the window restores selectivity enough to reach full resolution with the last peak still under 10 min.

The optimum appears centered near the 0.15–0.65, 10 min window, and the main unresolved lever left is a modest temperature shift around 40 C. Testing 45 C checks whether a small increase in temperature can keep the critical pair above 1.5 while shortening retention enough to retain a perfect score with potentially better practical speed.

A narrower, lower-end window improved the critical pair at 10 min, so combine that selectivity-favorable window with the shorter 8 min gradient to test whether it can recover full resolution while keeping the run faster. This directly probes whether window tuning can offset the loss in 6/7 resolution seen when only tG was shortened.

The 0.20–0.60 window gave stronger 6/7 resolution than 0.20–0.65 at 10 min, so it is the best candidate to support a shorter run from the high-phi0 side. Testing it at 8 min checks whether this shifted, narrowed window can retain full resolution while reducing run time further.

Most nearby window changes from the perfect methods have reduced the critical 6/7 resolution, so test the opposite direction by lowering phi0 one step below the original optimum while keeping phi1, tG, and T fixed. This checks whether giving the early part of the gradient more low-organic range can improve the decisive middle selectivity enough to maintain a perfect score.

We have mapped most of the local window around the optimum except the higher-phi0, narrower case. Testing 0.25–0.60 at 10 min and 40 C checks whether a further upward-shifted, trimmed window can still keep the critical pair resolved while pulling the last peak under 10 min.

The only nearby untested direction that could improve the critical 6/7 selectivity is a slightly lower, narrower window. Testing 0.10–0.55 at the proven 10 min and 40 C checks whether further trimming the high end can retain full resolution and perhaps bring the best pair margin/window balance.

Lowering phi1 to 0.55 greatly improved the critical-pair margin but was too slow from phi0 0.10, so shift the whole window upward to 0.15–0.55. This tests whether the stronger selectivity from the lower high end can be combined with a faster last peak to recover a perfect score.

The 0.55 high end consistently gives excellent resolution but is too slow; increasing phi0 has shortened runs in this system, so 0.20–0.55 is the key remaining local test. This checks whether the lower-phi1 selectivity advantage can be preserved while pulling the last peak closer to or under 10 min.

With only two injections left and multiple 1.000 methods already found, use one to probe a distinct higher-temperature, shallower variant near the best local window in case the critical pair recovers at a different slope-temperature combination. This explores a remaining interaction not yet tested around the near-optimal 0.20–0.65 region.

This is the main untested local window around the near-optimal region: higher phi0 shortened runs, while higher phi1 often brought t_last well below 10 min. It tests whether those two shifts together can recover full resolution of the critical 6/7 pair while maintaining a sub-10-minute last peak.
